questions.question:
**Identify the segment in the sentence which contains the grammatical error.**

He was surprised at me refusing his offer.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **__at me refusing__**

**__*Key Points__**

 
• **'at my refusing' **should be there in place of **'at me refusing'**
 
• **Possessive case of pronoun **comes before gerund for the following reason:
 
 
• The failure to use the possessive case with the gerund can create an illogical statement
 
• Consider the following sentence:
 
 
• I appreciate you taking time to talk with me about the project.

 ​The possessive case of *you* is not used with the gerund *taking*, so the writer ends up making the illogical statement (at least in this context) “I appreciate you.” The point is not that the writer of the sentence appreciates you,* per se; instead, the writer appreciates the fact that you took time to discuss the project: ​​
 
• I appreciate *your* taking time to talk with me about the project.​​​​​​
 
 
 
 

**Thus, the correct sentence is:* ****He was surprised at my refusing his offer.*

questions.question:
**Select the antonym of the given word.**

MOROSE
questions.solution:
Here the correct answer is **Cheerful.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The antonym of "**morose**" is "**cheerful**."
 
• The word "**morose**" means **being gloomy, sullen, and ill-tempered.** It is used to describe someone who is in a bad mood and is unwilling to engage in social interactions or conversations.
 
 
• Example: After losing his job, he became **morose **and stopped talking to his friends and family.
 
 
 
• "**Cheerful**" means being happy and optimistic, and it is the opposite of "morose."
 
 
• For example, "She was feeling **cheerful **after getting the job offer."
 
 
 
• In conclusion, the antonym of "morose" is "cheerful," which means happy and optimistic.
 
• Thus, the correct answer is Option 1.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Let's have a look at the **meaning **of other words in options:-

 
 
• "**Gloomy**" means dark or dim, or feeling sad or depressed. It is a synonym of "morose" and, therefore, not an antonym.
 
• "**Sick**" means feeling unwell, having a disease, or being unhealthy. It is not an antonym of "morose."
 
• "**Tasteless**" means lacking in flavor or character or lacking in aesthetic quality. It is not an antonym of "morose."** **

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select No improvement.**

The man who __seen the accident to occur__ telephoned the police.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Option 3 i.e. **"had seen the accident occur".**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The phrase **"had seen" **correctly implies that the witnessing of the accident occurred **before the action of telephoning** the police.
 
• When **two incidents happen** in **the past one by one**, we use **past perfect tense for the first incident** and **simple past for the second incident.**
 
• **Here accident had occurred first then the man telephoned.**
 
• The structure **"had seen the accident occur"** correctly uses the **past perfect tense** to indicate the sequence of events.

Therefore, the correct answer is-* "The man who **had seen the accident occur__** telephoned the police."*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1 ("saw the accident was occurring")** implies that the accident was in the process of happening, but is awkward and does not clearly convey that the action of seeing was completed before he telephoned.
 
• **Option 2 ("saw the accident occurred") **is grammatically incorrect because "saw" and "occurred" do not correctly align in a sequence of events.

questions.question:

questions.solution:

*It is blue in colour.*

'They' is used to refer to two or more people or things. 

For example:

*They were in the room a minute ago.*

'Them' is used as the object of a verb or preposition to refer to two or more people.

questions.question:

The plant will die ________ you look after it.
questions.solution:
Here, first understand the difference between the words (subordinating conjunctions) mentioned in the options.

"**If**" means "in the event of something".

For Example: *If it is sunny tomorrow, we can go to the park.*

"**Unless**" means "except, on the condition":

For Example: *You will not pass the exam unless you work harder.*

"**Otherwise" **means "apart from that"

For example: *Walk slowly on the ice, otherwise, you'll fall.*

"**Until**" means "up to the time that"

For Example: *Don't do anything until I come back.*

In the statement, if you don't take care, the plant will die. That means if care is not taken, it will die. So the correct conjunction will be "unless".

Hence, the correct answer will be option 2.

questions.question:
**Identify the segment in the sentence, which contains the grammatical error.**

Neither Mohit nor Rohit were there at the shop when I went there.
questions.solution:
The erroneous part is: **were there**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• 'Neither' and 'nor' are** correlative conjunctions** i.e., they are always used in **pair**.
 
• In case of **'neither…nor'**, always put **verb** according to the **subject** which is **closest**.
 
 
• For example: Neither my friends nor **I** **am** coming to meet you. (The verb 'am' is used as it is closest to the subject 'I')
 
 
 
• Similarly, in this context, the verb must agree with 'Rohit' (singular subject).
 
• Hence, 'was' (singular verb) must replace 'were' (plural verb).

Therefore, the correct answer is: *Neither Mohit nor Rohit** was** there at the shop when I went there.*

* [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__***

 
• Also, in case of **either…or**, always put the **verb** according to the **subject **which is **closest.**

 
 
• For example: Either my friends or **I am** coming to meet you. (In this sentence, the verb “am” agrees with the subject “I” because it is closest to it.)

• **Pretend** means to behave falsely.
 
• **Prefer** means likely to choose something.
 
• **Prepare **means to make something ready for use or consideration.
 
• **Pester** means to behave in an annoying manner.

 

We can see that the meaning of "**feign**" is related to pretending, so the correct answer will be '**pretend**.'
